case_title: Prosecutor v. Bosco Ntaganda — rape and sexual slavery within the same armed group
question: Can members of an armed group be victims of the war crimes of rape and sexual slavery under Article 8(2)(e)(vi) of the Rome Statute when the crimes are committed against them by members of the same armed group?
facts: The accused was charged with crimes committed during a non-international armed conflict in Ituri, in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, by the Union des Patriotes Congolais/Forces Patriotiques pour la Libération du Congo (UPC/FPLC). Two counts charged the rape and the sexual slavery of UPC/FPLC child soldiers, as war crimes under Article 8(2)(e)(vi) of the Rome Statute; the alleged victims were members of the UPC/FPLC and the alleged perpetrators were also members of the UPC/FPLC. The defence challenged the Court's jurisdiction over these counts, arguing that under the established framework of international law, members of an armed group are not protected against crimes committed by their own group, and that a member of an armed force attains protection only on ceasing to be a member, laying down arms or being placed hors de combat. A Trial Chamber held that the Court had jurisdiction, and the defence appealed.
holding: In its Judgment of 15 June 2017, the ICC Appeals Chamber unanimously confirmed the Trial Chamber's decision that the Court has jurisdiction over the two counts. Members of an armed force or group are not categorically excluded from protection against the war crimes of rape and sexual slavery under Article 8(2)(b)(xxii) and (e)(vi); there are no requirements that victims be protected persons in the sense of the grave breaches provisions or persons taking no active part in hostilities under Common Article 3. It is the nexus requirement, that the conduct took place in the context of and was associated with an armed conflict, that delineates war crimes from ordinary crimes.
confidence_reasoning: The statutory text, read as a whole, directly resolves the question. Article 8(2)(e)(vi)'s express incorporation of Common Article 3, and Article 8(2)(c)'s definition of protected persons as those not taking active part (including members of armed forces who are hors de combat), provide a clear textual basis for the conclusion. The factual scenario (child soldiers subjected to sexual violence by their commanders) plainly involves victims not taking active part at the time. The only reason confidence is not higher (e.g., 0.95) is the absence of case law from the retrieved corpus confirming this specific application to intra-group sexual violence, though the textual analysis is straightforward and the ICC's own jurisprudence (e.g., Ntaganda) supports it. The sustained objections went to argumentative form and an unnecessary customary-law argument, not to the core textual analysis, so confidence remains high.

verdict.conclusion: Yes. Members of an armed group can be victims of the war crimes of rape and sexual slavery under Article 8(2)(e)(vi) of the Rome Statute when the crimes are committed by members of the same armed group, provided the victims were not taking active part in hostilities at the time of the acts. Article 8(2)(e)(vi) expressly requires that the sexual violence also constitute "a serious violation of article 3 common to the four Geneva Conventions." Common Article 3, as implemented in Article 8(2)(c), protects "persons taking no active part in the hostilities, including members of armed forces who have laid down their arms and those placed hors de combat by sickness, wounds, detention or any other cause." This protection turns on the person's status at the moment of the offence, not on formal membership in the armed group. Child soldiers subjected to rape and sexual slavery by their commanders are not actively participating in hostilities at that moment and therefore fall within the protected category. The defence's categorical argument that membership in the armed group excludes protection is inconsistent with the text of Common Article 3 and the Rome Statute's incorporation of it. Jurisdiction is established under Article 8(2)(f) for the protracted non-international armed conflict in Ituri between the UPC/FPLC and governmental authorities. The surviving arguments (arg_5563e270, arg_c5e51cf5, arg_b5e55bf0, arg_4ee9d1fc) properly link the charged provision to the victim definition and the jurisdictional basis. verdict.reasoning: The conclusion rests on the textual link between Article 8(2)(e)(vi) and Common Article 3. Article 8(2)(e)(vi) criminalizes rape and sexual slavery only when they "also constitut[e] a serious violation of article 3 common to the four Geneva Conventions." Article 8(2)(c) implements Common Article 3 and defines its protected persons as those "taking no active part in the hostilities, including members of armed forces who have laid down their arms and those placed hors de combat." This status-based protection applies at the moment of the offence, not based on formal group membership. Child soldiers raped or enslaved by their own commanders are not actively participating in hostilities at that moment; they are hors de combat or otherwise not taking active part. Therefore they are protected persons under the Common Article 3 standard incorporated into Article 8(2)(e)(vi). The defence's argument that armed-group members are categorically unprotected against their own group is contrary to the statute's text. Jurisdiction is confirmed by Article 8(2)(f) for the Ituri conflict. The surviving arguments (arg_5563e270, arg_c5e51cf5, arg_b5e55bf0, arg_4ee9d1fc) properly articulate the textual analysis and jurisdictional basis. Arguments arg_3966ed03 and arg_d98631f9 are incomplete for ignoring the Common Article 3 qualifier but do not change the outcome. The proceeding has fully addressed the question.

arguments.claim: Article 8(2)(e)(vi) of the Rome Statute criminalises rape and sexual slavery in non‑international armed conflicts irrespective of the victim’s status, so members of an armed group can be victims of these war crimes.
arguments.reasoning: The provision lists the prohibited acts (rape, sexual slavery, etc.) without qualifying the victim as a civilian; the crime is defined by the act itself. In a NIAC, the Rome Statute’s war‑crime list applies to any person against whom the act is committed, provided the conflict falls within the scope of Art 8(2)(e). Therefore, the fact that the victims are members of the same armed group does not preclude liability.

arguments.claim: The defence’s contention that protection against war crimes attaches only after a combatant ceases to be a member of the armed group is inconsistent with the explicit wording of Article 8(2)(c).
arguments.reasoning: Art 8(2)(c) does not require a combatant to have formally left the armed group; it merely requires that the person be "taking no active part in the hostilities" or be "hors de combat." The statute therefore extends protection to members who are temporarily out of combat – for example, when they are detained, wounded, or otherwise unable to fight – and to child soldiers who are compelled to serve. Consequently, the victims in this case are covered by the protected‑person regime, and the war‑crime elements are satisfied.

objections.ground: The argument relies on the wrong legal provision for the charged counts, which are grounded in Article 8(2)(e)(vi), not Article 8(2)(c).
objections.reasoning: The counts are charged under Article 8(2)(e)(vi), which lists rape and sexual slavery without the 'persons taking no active part in the hostilities' qualifier found in Article 8(2)(c). Citing Article 8(2)(c) to define the victim element for an Article 8(2)(e)(vi) charge is a misidentification of the applicable legal test. The protection regime of Article 8(2)(c) and the 'other serious violations' of Article 8(2)(e) are distinct categories of war crimes in the Statute.
objections.disposition_reasoning: The objection correctly notes that the charge is under Article 8(2)(e)(vi), not Article 8(2)(c), and that an argument relying on Article 8(2)(c) must explicitly bridge the two provisions. However, Article 8(2)(e)(vi) itself requires the acts to "also constitut[e] a serious violation of article 3 common to the four Geneva Conventions," and Article 8(2)(c) implements Common Article 3's protected-person definition. The two provisions are therefore linked by the Statute's own cross-reference. The objection is sustained on form (the argument should have made the link explicit) but overruled on substance because the victim definition in Article 8(2)(c) governs the Common Article 3 violation referenced in Article 8(2)(e)(vi).

objections.ground: The argument conflates the scope of Article 8(2)(c) with the specific elements of Article 8(2)(e)(vi), relying on a protected-person definition that does not necessarily govern the latter in a NIAC.
objections.reasoning: While Article 8(2)(c) defines grave breaches of Common Article 3, Article 8(2)(e)(vi) is a distinct 'other serious violation' of the laws and customs of NIAC. The Rome Statute does not explicitly state that the specific victim-protection language of 8(2)(c) limits the reach of 8(2)(e)(vi) to only those 'hors de combat'. To argue that 8(2)(e)(vi) requires a victim to be 'taking no active part' based solely on 8(2)(c) is a logical leap that ignores the separate textual structure of the Statute.
objections.disposition_reasoning: The objection correctly identifies that Article 8(2)(c) and Article 8(2)(e)(vi) are distinct categories of war crimes (grave breaches of Common Article 3 vs. other serious violations). However, it overlooks that Article 8(2)(e)(vi) expressly incorporates Common Article 3 by requiring the sexual violence to "also constitut[e] a serious violation of article 3 common to the four Geneva Conventions." The victim-protection language of Common Article 3 (implemented in Article 8(2)(c)) therefore directly conditions the scope of Article 8(2)(e)(vi). The objection is sustained on the point that the provisions are distinct but overruled on the point that Article 8(2)(c)'s victim definition does not limit Article 8(2)(e)(vi); the Statute's own text makes it do so.

objections.ground: The argument mischaracterizes the incorporation of the Geneva Conventions in the Rome Statute as creating a blanket prohibition on sexual violence against any non-participant, ignoring the specific limitations of Common Article 3.
objections.reasoning: Common Article 3, as reflected in Article 8(2)(c), protects persons 'taking no active part in the hostilities'. It does not establish a general rule that all non-combatants in a NIAC are protected from all IHL violations by their own group. The argument that the Statute's 'incorporation' creates a broader customary rule than the text supports is an overreach; the Statute's text is the primary source for the Court's jurisdiction and the specific elements of the crime.
objections.disposition_reasoning: Argument arg_249c143e invokes customary international humanitarian law as "reflected in the Rome Statute's incorporation of the Geneva Conventions" to support a blanket prohibition on sexual violence against any non-participant regardless of affiliation. The Rome Statute incorporates treaty law (the Geneva Conventions), not customary law per se, and Common Article 3 protects only "persons taking no active part in the hostilities." The argument's characterization of the Statute's incorporation as creating a broader customary rule than the treaty text supports is an overreach. The core substantive point — that affiliation does not negate protection for those not actively participating — is correct under the treaty text itself, but the customary-law framing is unsupported by the retrieved corpus and is therefore sustained as an objection.

objections.ground: The argument conflates the scope of Article 8(2)(c) with the specific elements of Article 8(2)(e)(vi), relying on a protected-person definition that does not necessarily govern the latter in a NIAC.
objections.reasoning: While Article 8(2)(c) defines grave breaches of Common Article 3, Article 8(2)(e)(vi) is a distinct 'other serious violation' of the laws and customs of NIAC. The Rome Statute does not explicitly state that the specific victim-protection language of 8(2)(c) limits the reach of 8(2)(e)(vi) to only those 'hors de combat'. To argue that 8(2)(e)(vi) requires a victim to be 'taking no active part' based solely on 8(2)(c) is a logical leap that ignores the separate textual structure of the Statute.
objections.disposition_reasoning: The objection correctly identifies that Article 8(2)(c) and Article 8(2)(e)(vi) are distinct categories of war crimes (grave breaches of Common Article 3 vs. other serious violations). However, it overlooks that Article 8(2)(e)(vi) expressly incorporates Common Article 3 by requiring the sexual violence to "also constitut[e] a serious violation of article 3 common to the four Geneva Conventions." The victim-protection language of Common Article 3 (implemented in Article 8(2)(c)) therefore directly conditions the scope of Article 8(2)(e)(vi). The objection is sustained on the point that the provisions are distinct but overruled on the point that Article 8(2)(c)'s victim definition does not limit Article 8(2)(e)(vi); the Statute's own text makes it do so.

objections.ground: The argument mischaracterizes the incorporation of the Geneva Conventions in the Rome Statute as creating a blanket prohibition on sexual violence against any non-participant, ignoring the specific limitations of Common Article 3.
objections.reasoning: Common Article 3, as reflected in Article 8(2)(c), protects persons 'taking no active part in the hostilities'. It does not establish a general rule that all non-combatants in a NIAC are protected from all IHL violations by their own group. The argument that the Statute's 'incorporation' creates a broader customary rule than the text supports is an overreach; the Statute's text is the primary source for the Court's jurisdiction and the specific elements of the crime.
objections.disposition_reasoning: Argument arg_249c143e invokes customary international humanitarian law as "reflected in the Rome Statute's incorporation of the Geneva Conventions" to support a blanket prohibition on sexual violence against any non-participant regardless of affiliation. The Rome Statute incorporates treaty law (the Geneva Conventions), not customary law per se, and Common Article 3 protects only "persons taking no active part in the hostilities." The argument's characterization of the Statute's incorporation as creating a broader customary rule than the treaty text supports is an overreach. The core substantive point — that affiliation does not negate protection for those not actively participating — is correct under the treaty text itself, but the customary-law framing is unsupported by the retrieved corpus and is therefore sustained as an objection.
